analysis.one_liner: Forces giant online platforms to let users and businesses take their data and connect with competitors.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in June 2021, but it never received a vote in the House or Senate before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require very large online platforms — those with at least 50 million U.S. users or 100,000 business users, owned by a company worth more than $600 billion — to let people securely take their data to a competing service, and to open their systems so other platforms can connect and work with them. The Federal Trade Commission or Justice Department would designate which platforms are covered and write specific technical standards for each. Violations could cost a company up to 15% of its U.S. revenue, and repeat offenders' CEOs could forfeit a year of pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who could switch services without losing their photos, contacts, or history; small businesses that sell through dominant platforms and currently cannot leave or reach customers elsewhere; and smaller tech companies that could build compatible services.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, small businesses, and smaller tech competitors

how_it_helps.text: Covered platforms must maintain interfaces to securely transfer user data to users or, with their consent, to business users, in a structured, machine-readable format [S3].
Covered platforms must keep interoperability interfaces so competing businesses can connect to their systems on fair and nondiscriminatory terms, and must document how to access them [S3].
The FTC may recover civil penalties of up to 15% of a company's total U.S. revenue, or 30% of the affected line of business's revenue, plus restitution and disgorgement of unjust gains [S3].
For repeat violations, a court must consider requiring the platform's CEO to forfeit a year of compensation to the Treasury [S3].
The bill directs the FTC to write standards aimed at reducing the network effects that make it hard to compete with a dominant platform [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The large platforms designated as covered — companies exceeding $600 billion in market value — would pay to build and maintain open interfaces, face penalties up to 15% of U.S. revenue for violations, and lose some of the switching costs that keep users and advertisers on their services.

drawbacks.text: Opening interfaces to outside companies creates security and privacy risks; the bill addresses this by requiring businesses that receive data to secure it and allowing the FTC to cut off access to violators [S3].
The FTC would take on a heavy rulemaking workload, writing platform-by-platform interoperability standards and policing interface changes, which could be slow and technically difficult [S3].
Penalties as large as 15% of total U.S. revenue, applied to what is an 'unfair method of competition' violation, could fall heavily even on smaller compliance mistakes by covered companies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: a handful of platforms control access to customers and make it costly to leave, which limits competition. The costs fall on a small set of the largest companies, not on the public. The genuine risks are privacy and security holes in opened interfaces and an FTC rulemaking process that could be slow or clumsy — the bill attempts to manage both with data-security duties, emergency cutoff authority, and a technical advisory committee, but its heaviest penalty structure is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee marked it up and approved it in June 2021, but no one brought it to the House floor for a vote, and it never got one in the Senate before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill in the House on June 11, 2021, joined by Representatives Owens, Cicilline, Buck, and Nadler [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on June 11, 2021 [S1].
The committee held markup sessions on June 23 and 24, 2021, and on June 24 ordered the bill to be reported to the House with amendments [S5].
The action history ends with the committee approval; the bill was never reported to the full House for a vote [S5].
The bill gathered 28 cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 9 Republicans [S4].
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2023, without the bill reaching a floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant online platforms came out ahead: they keep the switching costs and closed systems the bill would have ended, and face no new interoperability requirements or penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dominant online platforms that avoided the rules

industries.industry: Large online platforms (companies over $600 billion in market value)
industries.note: The bill would force these companies to open their systems to competitors and let users leave with their data, with penalties up to 15% of U.S. revenue. Their business depends on high switching costs and closed access to users, so their interest runs against the competition the bill would create for consumers and small merchants.
Interoperability would let smaller services connect to dominant platforms and compete for users without building everything from scratch, which is also what gives consumers more choices.

industries.industry: Businesses that sell through dominant platforms
industries.note: Merchants and app developers currently cannot easily move their customer relationships off a dominant platform; portability and interoperability would lower that cost.
